Let's wrangle the iris dataset with some useful functions:
-filter() remember "==" means equal to and "!=" means note equal to
-mutate()

```{r}
dataframe_1 <- df %>% 
  filter(Species == "versicolor")
  

dataframe_2 <- iris %>% 
  filter((Species == "versicolor") | (Species == "virginica"))

dataframe_3 <- iris %>% 
  filter(Species != "setosa")
# == vs !=

dataframe_4 <- dataframe_3 %>% 
  mutate(petal_shape = Petal.Length/Petal.Width)

dataframe_5 <- iris %>% 
  filter(Species != "setosa") %>% 
  mutate(petal_shape = Petal.Length/Petal.Width)


```


Let's model data YAAAAAAAAY!!!!!!

```{r}
# Note that standard deviations are modeled to represent a coefficient of variation (CV) of 15%. That is, the standard deviation is 15% the size of the mean. This is a typical CV for samples that are normally distributed.

# all masses are in kilograms

# Modeling an Experiment
mouth_size <- rnorm(n = 25, mean = 8.5, sd = 1.275)
largemouth <- as.data.frame(mouth_size) %>% 
  mutate(fish_type = "Largemouth Bass")

mouth_size <- rnorm(n = 32, mean = 7.2, sd = 1.08)
spotted <- as.data.frame(mouth_size) %>% 
  mutate(fish_type = "Spotted Bass")

demo_data <- largemouth %>% 
  bind_rows(spotted) %>% 
  rename("IV" = 'fish_type', "DV" = 'mouth_size') 

# How do you model a different example but show the null hypothesis?

```

Graph your modeled data to visualize

```{r}
demo_data %>% 
  # filter(DV > 5) |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = IV, y = DV)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  labs(title = "Bass Mouth Size")

demo_data %>% 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = IV, y = DV)) +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0) +
  labs(title = "Bass Mouth Size")
```
